entities.summary:
Angelo Cino (b. 1350, Bevagna – d. June 30, 1412, Bevagna) emerged as a significant ecclesiastical figure within the turbulent landscape of late Medieval Italy, serving primarily as the Bishop of Gravina and later as Bishop of Osimo. His career unfolded amidst the profound challenges of the Western Schism (1378–1417), a period that fractured the authority of the Roman Catholic Church and forced loyalties to be declared between rival popes. Cino's administrative acumen and diplomatic engagement were instrumental in navigating these complex ecclesiastical and political currents, impacting the spiritual and temporal affairs of the dioceses under his charge within the Papal States.

Elevated to the episcopacy by Pope Boniface IX in 1390 as Bishop of Gravina, Cino quickly demonstrated a capacity for governance beyond mere spiritual oversight, engaging with local nobility and municipal authorities to secure the church's interests and maintain order. His subsequent transfer to the more prominent See of Osimo in 1409, under Pope Gregory XII, further underscored his standing. During his tenure, Cino was deeply involved in the local administration of justice, the management of church properties, and the promotion of religious discipline, often contending with the pervasive influence of powerful noble families and the constant threat of factional strife that characterized central Italy at the time. He was a participant in the Council of Pisa in 1409, an ultimately unsuccessful attempt to resolve the Western Schism, demonstrating his direct engagement with the highest levels of church politics.
